I am very glad of that, because I noticed yesterday the observation that I had made that statement. The purpose of the government was to appoint a Canadian to that position but not to do so unless we could appoint him several months before his duties would commence in order that he might go abroad into countries where central banks existed so that he might be able to obtain the requisite experience to enable him to discharge the duties and functions of his position. It is idle to say that he can secure the information on this side of the water, for the central bank system as practised in the United States would not be of assistance for one undertaking the duties of governor of a central bank as indicated in the measure.
I leave this thought in the minds of the committee. It has -been pointed out on many occasions in the committee on banking and commerce and in this committee of the whole house that the bankers of this country have vigorously opposed this legislation. In fact, in their annual meetings you will find speeches directed against this central bank. I ask this

committee whether they think any government would have a free hand if it had to appoint to such positions those whose object would be unfavourable to and who in fact tried to destroy the central bank. That is the question, and that phase of the matter must be considered. The government therefore have sought a free hand in dealing with that question. If we can obtain in Canada any person qualified by experience in commercial banking and able to leave this country for the purpose of obtaining at least a few months' experience by observation in connection with matters concerned with a central bank, one who is not opposed to a central bank, then of course he will be appointed. But the important thing is that we must not appoint to that position anyone who is unsympathetic and who desires to destroy the venture and to make it a failure, and we do not propose to do so. Therefore we must have a free hand in dealing with the matter. It is equally probable that if we can secure a suitable person as assistant who has had a lifelong experience as a central bank authority to assist a general manager or governor experienced as I have indicated, we would desire and I believe any government would desire to do so.
In view of the observations made this afternoon I want to repeat what I said yesterday. You will not find in any records of central banks, that is banks similar to this-I am not talking about publicly owned banks; I am talking about banks whose shares are held by private individuals and the control of which is vested in the government as I indicated last night-any case in which the control is more certain and in which the inducement to those who are directors as representing shareholders will be greater to discharge an important public trust in a manner befitting the obligation that is imposed upon them. Why? Because they know they will receive nothing more than four and a half per cent upon their money; that no effort upon their part can increase this; that it merely adds to the sum total of the profits that go to the Dominion of Canada and in their patriotic zeal to serve a great public trust with fidelity I am quite certain there will be found in this country those who, will be not only willing but anxious to discharge so great an obligation in a manner befitting the magnitude of the work they will have to undertake. This is not a case in which they are seeking profit as it is in that of some of the central banks that are privately owned in the older countries. There their dividends may vary from six to eight, ten and twelve pier cent and,

Bank of Canada
as is known, in older countries the dividends of the bank run eighteen, twenty, twenty-three per cent. Here there is merely a modest return of four and a half per cent fixed upon the capital invested, and as I have pointed out I may misjudge, but I think I do not and I believe the zeal of those who are charged with this responsibility to do something to discharge a great public trust in a fitting manner will be manifested by the success which will attend their efforts. In the selection of officials, in the selection of governor, deputy governor and assistant, that object will be constantly in mind whether it be on the part of the governor in council or of the shareholders.
Last evening the leader of the opposition made an observation which I thought I heard correctly but which I verified in Hansard at page 4196 where he is reported as saying:
If you alter the situation by taking away from the government the power that it has to-day; and the banks are to be allowed to control the central bank-for that is what it really amounts to, the banking interest are all to be one, the central bank being in private hands; let us put it that way-there is, it seems to me, a real danger of the financial control which may thus be exercised by the bank being exercised against what may be the fiscal policy of the government of the day.
It is difficult for me to find in the same number of words a more inept conception of the real policy of the statute itself. Not only do the banks not own or control the central bank, but the statute in terms prohibits banks or bankers from owning shares in the central bank. It was that fear that the right hon. gentleman has expressed that is at the bottom of the provisions in the statute to prevent the bankers from exercising control over the central bank. I cannot conceive of any clearer statement being made than that contained in the bill in the clauses that will be dealt with this evening where there is a prohibition against any directing officer, clerk or employee of any bank being interested directly or indirectly or through the medium of anyone else, in this central bank. The restricted control by any individual or group of individuals is further indicated by the limitation imposed upon the shareholders: no one can hold in the institution more than fifty shares. I mention that because possibly the right hon. gentleman overlooked the provisions of the statute in that regard.
When it is indicated that the government is parting to a certain extent with the control it has over the regulation of credit I only desire to point out that for the first time in the history of Canada we are setting up an organization in which the control of the government over credit is real. I know the hon. member for Shelburne-Yarmouth did not overlook the fact that in all the advances made to the banks under the Finance Act, there is no coverage of the money advanced; under the Finance Act all the money advanced was without coverage.
Without gold backing.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Without gold backing or metal coverage. The only support it had was the security of bonds or other securities mentioned in the Finance Act itself.
Without the requirement for gold coverage because as a matter of fact it did have gold coverage; for, as I understand it, there is about forty per cent gold backing for all the notes issued.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
There was not until the borrowings under the Finance Act became very much restricted. When the borrowings under that act went to $66,000,000 in 1931, there was no metal or gold coverage that would approximate forty per cent. But the point is this-and I think it has been overlooked-this bank when it begins to function must maintain twenty-five per cent gold coverage for all of its note issue. Whether it be by way of loans or advances to those who come into the bank seeking them, or whether it be for the deposits or other business of the bank, it is compelled under the statute to hold twenty-five per cent gold coverage. That differentiates it from the conditions that exist under the Finance Act. I am not going to do more than say that heretofore in this country the members of this house, both those opposite and those to my extreme right, were always insistent, and I have never controverted the soundness of their statement, that the chartered banks really exercise control over credit, and under the Finance Act as it now stands their control over credit became more and more apparent as they relied more and more upon the provisions of the Finance Act. Under this bill the control of credit in truth and fact rests with the central bank, as it could not under the Finance Act.
I have looked through the provisions of the bill to determine whether or not there is any that I could see under which, the bank could operate to the detriment of any policy, fiscal or otherwise, which the government of the day might have. My judgment, for what it may be worth, and I offer it after having looked over the bill again, is that the Bank of Canada cannot control the mechanism used by the government for the purposes of its policy under any circumstances whatever.

Bank of Canada
The government promulgates its policies, whatever they may be; the central bank, an instrumentality of the government, assists in giving effect to those policies, carries them out in every way in its power; but surely it could have no jurisdiction under this or any other statute that I can conceive of with respect to a central bank that would enable it to interfere with or work at cross purposes with the government of the day in effecting its policies, whatever they may be. The ideas of the bank in regard to carrying on open market operations might conceivably be different from what an individual in the government might at the moment think, but I do not see how it could be said for a moment that they would in any way interfere with the general policies of administration. I have not been able by any process that I can rely upon to arrive at any such conclusion.
Would the Prime Minister permit me to interrupt here?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Certainly.

This is one point I have in mind: suppose the government of the day considered it advisable that the requirement of twenty-five per cent gold backing should be suspended, let us say for six months, in order that the issue of currency might increase, would it not be necessary for the privately appointed board first to pass a resolution providing for the suspension before the government could secure it?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
I have no doubt that
as the law stands the directors would take the initiative. But if it were a publicly owned bank with a board of directors the same course would have to be pursued.

Yes, but there would be
government directors on the board.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: But what assurance have you that the directors would discharge a public trust any more carefully because they are appointed by the government than if they are elected in the manner I have indicated?

Oh, if you take that
position there is no use in arguing.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
And with the four and
a half per cent limitation.

One has a good deal
more assurance than if they are appointed by private shareholders.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Have we? One has only to look at the history of one great publicly owned enterprise that we have had in this country to see. Certainly the evidence is

against that view. All you have to do is go down to the West Indies, and follow up from there to this country.

That has nothing to do
with the point.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: The point is that the directors would have to take the action in any event. Suspending the twenty-five per cent provision would be an act of the directors in the first instance. Under our provisions it would have to be approved by the government. If it were publicly owned the same procedure would follow, presumably, from what the hon. gentleman has said. He has not suggested that if it were a publicly owned bank and the directors were appointed by the government there would be any change in that part as far as the governor is concerned. Assuming that is as it is now, where would be the difference?

I think it is obvious, even if my right hon. friend cannot see it. If the directors were appointed by the government it would seem that they would be more likely to carry out the wishes of the government by whom they were appointed than would directors appointed by private shareholders.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
What the hon. gentleman suggests proves what I have contended from the start. This view is that the directors are not to think for themselves, that they are to be thought for and to be told what they are to do, without regard to their own views;-whereas in the other instance we imply some intelligent consideration of the questions at issue. There is no doubt that in both cases the initiative must come from the directors, acting in both instances on the request of the government of the day, and if they suggest the suspension of the twenty-five per cent gold coverage merely because a political group said it should be done, as against what their reason told them should be done in the interests of the nation as a whole, they would be reflecting a political judgment on the one hand as against a business judgment on the other. That is the whole story. That is what we have endeavoured to set our face against. The discussions that have taken place here indicate how readily the situation would become charged with danger for the bank itself, even as the situation would become charged with danger with directors who merely carried out the will of either one man or a group of men. That is the position. I am not going to traverse it further except to say that by no process of reasoning which I can apply to the facts and in no case of which I can conceive

Bank of Canada
would it be possible for this bank in any sense to balk or stand in the way of policies of a government being made effective in any manner that the government of the day thought in the public interest, whether fiscal or otherwise.

Mr. Chairman, the Prime Minister (Mr. Bennett) has not really answered my point beyond giving it as his individual opinion that there would be no possibility of conflict between this bank and the government. He has not given us reasons why such conflict of opinion might not arise. As members of the committee will recall, my point was that, in the absence of any directors appointed by the government, and with all directors being appointed by the shareholders, there might on occasions be no means of bringing about the necessary harmony between the government and the bank with respect to a course of procedure that might vitally affect some great national policy. I pointed out that I thought a case might arise where the bank, being a privately owned institution and privately controlled, and being associated with private banks in' other parts of the empire, might come to have one financial policy to which it would adhere very strongly, but that the government of the day, for very obvious national reasons, might desire to follow another policy, or to alter in some particular, essential to the national interest, the policy of the bank. The government might have a policy with respect to trade or shipping or some other great national service which would require the cooperation in a friendly way of the bank, and that would not be possible unless the government as well as the shareholders, was represented on the board of directors of the bank. The Prime Minister did say last night that there was the possibility that in time of crisis there might be a moment when there would appear to be conflict, but he thought it would work out all right. I wish I could be as sanguine as he is about everything working out all right. I can understand my right hon. friend having the feelings he has at this time about this phase of the situation; he is going to appoint the governor, he is going to appoint the deputy governor. The shareholders of this bank will appoint the directors, but the real control of the bank's affairs will be in the hands of his own appointee. The governor will be a gentleman, unquestionably, of the same point of view on financial and economic affairs as the right hon. Prime Minister himself. I know the Prime Minister is sincere in the views that he holds as regards both trade and finance, but, with all
respect and deference, I say to him that there are those who believe that his policies are wrong, and that the best interests of this countiy and of the empire would be furthered by policies wholly different from those which he cherishes at the moment. That is where I see the possibility some day of conflict between what may be the policies of this bank and the policies of the administration that may be in office.
I want to make this fact clear: no one could have had the responsibility of being the head of an administration for any time without realizing all that is meant when one speaks of political pressure. I think I would be the first to sympathize with the Prime Minister in his desire so to frame an act that what is termed political pressure would not be permitted to interfere with the successful and independent working of a great financial institution. May I say we may give a wholly wrong meaning to the word "political" in speaking of political pressure. A political influence or point of view is not necessarily something that is contrary to the national interest; a political point of view is one which arises from an endeavour to give expression to public feeling and public opinion, and I submit that in all democratic countries public opinion is the one great factor for which all governments must have consideration. There are times when it is necessary and vital that every institution in the land should be subject to the public opinion of the nation, and this is always the case when it is expressed in a constitutional way in parliament. I do not believe powers should be given any institution that would enable it to put itself in a position of opposition to a government that has been entrusted with great responsibilities of enforcing particular policies.
In order to be perfectly clear, I should like to assert the two definite sets of circumstances I have in mind. The first relates to a conflict which might arise between the government and the bank at any time of crisis regardless of what administration may be in office, a crisis which might arise from unforeseen economic conditions in the country itself. You would then have two powers that would come into conflict with each other; and unless there is some way of harmonizing them great mischief may be done. You have the money power represented by the central bank and you have the political power represented by the government. I am not one of those who is given to indulging in the extravagant language which is used in these times about money power and the terrors of international
Bank of Canada

banking and finance, blit no one can live in this day and age without realizing that we have in the money power of the world an invisible force which is all-powerful in different countries at the present time. What is being proposed under this legislation is that the government shall part with its control over the issue of currency and over national credit to a private corporation which is a great banking institution and which to a certain extent is to regulate the affairs of all other banks. When I say that the banldng institutions are to be all one, I do not mean that the central bank will be controlled by the chartered banks of the country. What I do mean to say is that all questions relating to currency and national credit will hereafter be in the hands of the central bank and other banks throughout the country and no longer in the hands of the government. They will be in the hands of the banking interests, which means in the hands of the financial interests, and parliament will have parted altogether with any control it has over the issue of currency or over credit. There are those who hold that when a nation parts with its control over currency and national credit, it does not matter very much who makes the laws of that nation. The power that controls the currency and the credit of the country is a power that, if there is such a thing at all as political influence of the kind referred to by the Prime Minister, can make itself felt upon governments.
I say that power of influence of governments and defiance of governments by the money power is being created by this act in the form in which it is at present, and the only way in which that possibility can be avoided is for the government to see to it that, on the board of directors who are to direct this institution, there are representatives of the government, who will not own any of the shares, but who will be the appointees of the government placed there solely to watch and safe guard the public interest. I think my right hon. friend must agree that in these matters of large finance, check and counter check is wholly advisable. It is advisable in financial transactions of a limited size, and it is more necessary as well as advisable in those of considerable size. But here are financial transactions of the greatest magnitude conceivable, and check and counter check are imperative. I do think the directorate of the bank ought to be so formed that, whether the pressure is upon the bank from the government on the one side, or upon the government from the financial interests and through the bank on

the other, there should be on the board of directors some one or more persons who will be quick to sense the situation, give the danger signal, and arouse the country to the pressure which is being brought to bear. There is the danger of a government bringing too much in the way of pressure to bear on a central bank. On the other hand, there is equal danger of the financial interests that are allied with the banks bringing influence to bear upon a government. There will be both these dangers always, and the only way in which that possibility can be lessened is by making sure that both powers, the money power and the power of government, are represented on a common board so that one or the other will be in a position to direct the attention of the people at large to the dangers which they may see developing in the affairs of an institution which is or ought to be a great national trust.
May I now direct attention to the other set of circumstances I have in mind, namely, the difficulties that I see which may arise in carrying out national policies when there is a change of administration. Here I want to differ absolutely from and to take issue with the Prime Minister in what he said last night. In order that I may not misinterpret what he said after I had asked for an explanation as to a certain point, I shall quote the words of my right hon. friend as they appear at page 4195 of Hansard:
If the government were in complete control of the bank it would mean that if you had one government succeeded by another the bank would naturally change its policy, assuming that the policy was as the right hon. gentleman suggested. Then you would have governments controlling policies without continuity. What we wish to secure is a policy based upon the economic conditions of the country, not a policy of the bank based upon policies of a government. That is what the right hon. gentleman desires.
What I should like to ask is: Are the institutions created by governments themselves to be made by their very constitutions so powerful that in the matter of national policies they can regard themselves as wholly beyond the direction of a government, where those policies are the result of the will of the people as expressed by their representatives in parliament? In no way could it be possible to have more clearly defined the difference between the right hon. gentleman opposite and myself. The Prime Minister will notice that at the moment, I am not suggesting the government should own the bank. I am not at the moment discussing the question of ownership, at all. As I said last night, I think

Bank of Canada
the question of ownership is debatable. I am however discussing the question of control of policy, and I do say that with respect to policies, whether they relate to trade, to shipping, to marketing, to finance, to defence, or to any other phase of a country's economy, those policies, if they are the expression of view of a government representative of the people, should be capable of being carried out without interference from any institution whatever, but rather with the sympathetic cooperation of all institutions. That is the only way in which in a country we can have either democratic or responsible government.
I should like to be very frank and concrete in what I am saying, and in order that the Prime Minister will not think I am in any way seeking to misinterpret his point of view or the point of view of any hon. gentleman opposite, I should like first of all to present the matter as I think he sees it. He knows that he will have the appointment of the governor and of the deputy governor of the bank, and he knows also that those who are likely to be appointed as directors will be governed very largely by the point of view of the governor of the bank. He has asserted -although I believe this evening there has been some modification-that the governor would in all probability be some one who would come from the old country.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: No, I have not modified any statement with respect to the governor.
What I have said I believe still stands. I think to-night my right hon. friend did go as far as to say that possibly a Canadian could be found for the position.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: I said that yesterday, too.
I beg your pardon?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: The right hon. gentleman did not follow me. My statement is in Hansard. What I said was that without experience which could be gained by giving him an opportunity, there was no one in Canada who I thought at the moment could be appointed. I said if there were an appointment made tomorrow it would have to be made under circumstances which would enable the appointee to have five or six months' experience in England, or elsewhere.

I shall not discuss the question whether or not the one to be appointed governor is to be one whose residence has been in England or in Canada. For the purposes of my argument it is sufficient to say that the Prime Minister will appoint
the governor, and that he will appoint someone who, he believes, holds sound views on economic and financial questions, and views which are sound because in accordance with his own. I believe that is a reasonable assumption.
A few evenings ago, I spoke about an imperial trade policy, and the Prime Minister took strong exception to the use of the word "imperial." He said that I was seeking through the use of that word to create some prejudice. I used it because it is the word in common use to signify what is meant. I notice the right hon. gentleman said he had not used it, but I looked up his language in. the particular address he delivered, and-

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
I did not use it that
night.
Mr. MACKENZIE. KING:	Not that
night. I find what he did use in the address I refer to was the expression "common policy," and by a common policy he meant a policy for all parts of the empire. To my way of thinking a common policy for all parts of the empire is what is meant when we speak of an 'imperial policy. The word "imperial" expresses in a very short, concise and complete manner what is meant by the expression "a common policy for all parts of the British Empire." I believe the Prime Minister-and he has never denied it-believes in his heart of hearts that in the matter of trade a common policy for all parts of the British Empire would be in the best interests of the peoples of the British Empire, and I believe further that his tariff policies have been designed towards the end of bringing about a common trade policy throughout the different parts of the empire. That is his point of view, and he is entitled to it. I wish he would debate the matter openly, and let us argue the question as to whether or not that policy would be as good for Canada as what we describe as a world trade policy. A world trade policy, not an empire trade policy, represents the point of view held by hon. gentlemen on this side of the house. We do not believe that the interests of the British Empire, and those of Canada in particular, are going to be furthered by any common trade policies for all parts of the empire, whether they be called imperial or common policies, or by any other name. We believe in a policy of trading with any and every nation that will trade with us, as best for the empire and best for Canada as a part of the empire. Let us assume that the appointee to the position of governor of the bank would be a gentleman holding the same point of view as is held by the Prime Minister,

Bank of Canada
honestly believing that the right thing to do is to encourage trade within the British Empire and to develop channels of trade throughout the different parts of the empire so that for the most part trade would necessarily flow in empire channels rather than between this country and countries, generally, throughout the world. Is it not altogether probable that the governor of the central bank would find it possible to further that common or imperial trade policy by the opportunities which would be afforded him and his institution, as for example, in dealing with matters of exchange? Would he not, by artificial means, through the manipulation of exchange, be in a position to further the policy which the government has in view, and which, in matters of trade, he and the Prime Minister would hold in common? I am perfectly sure that an institution of the character of a central bank which has to do with a nation's credit, which has to do with the issuing of the nation's currency, which has to do with the regulation of exchange and with great problems of international exchange, could, by artificial means, direct the trade of this country through particular channels and away from other channels.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
May I say to the right
hon. gentleman that that could be done only by parliament giving them the money with which to do it. The stabilization of exchange could not be done without the aid of parliament.

The Prime
Minister may seek to answer in that way. I believe he is beginning to see the force of what I am saying. In connection with imperial policies of trade or finance may I observe that both are clearly and closely interlocked. No one knows better than the Prime Minister that the facilities which banks afford to importers and exporters determine very largely in what direction and from what sources trade is to flow. Look at the picture as it is beginning to disclose itself. We have, first of all the Bank of England, which stands at the centre. Then there are the central banking institutions already in existence in Australia, New Zealand and South Africa. I believe it is a fact that at the head of each one of these central banks is a gentleman associated- with the Bank of England, or one who has had previous associations with the bank of England. If in Canada we have at the head of our central bank another gentleman who has been trained by the Bank of England, and whose associations are with that bank, what would be more natural than that these central banks within the British empire,

all trained from the London point of view, and all embued with the idea that a great imperial or intraempire trade is the thing to be fostered, should do their utmost further to develop trade in that way to the exclusion of every other? As I say, so long as the Prime Minister, himself, is in office, I can see how he may well entertain the view that there is not likely to be any danger experienced of a character which would lead to any conflict between his government and this new banking institution. But let us assume for a moment that there is a change of administration, and let us assume that a government is in office in Canada which wishes to develop trade throughout the world, trade by Canada, with all the nations of the world, foreign as well as British nations, and does not believe it to be restricted by artificial means in the interests either of Canada or of the empire to have trade so as to confine it mostly to channels within the British Empire. Then according to the Prime Minister's reasoning, and the grounds he adduced for giving this bank the constitution he is giving to it, we are face to face with this following situation:	The bank is to
maintain continuity in its financial policy- an imperial financial policy to support an imperial trade policy-and is not on any account to change its policy because there has come into office a government with other policies which have been approved by the people. The words are as plain as the English language can make them. The Prime Minister said:
What we wish to secure is a policy based on the economic conditions of the country, not a bank based on the policies of the government.
The policies that any government would have would be policies based on the economic conditions of the country, especially where they were policies that had been presented to the people, and which the people had approved, and which as a consequence the people would have a right to expect that every institution which exists in the land would harmoniously help to further to the largest possible extent. I see there a very great danger. Possibly the Prime Minister will come back with this reply, that parliament can always alter the statute which it has made. But, as he himself is so fond of saying, we are obliged to deal with conditions and not with theories, and we know that parliament consists of two houses and that the approval of both houses is necessary to the amendment of any statute. We know that at the present time the other house of parliament is one which represents very strongly the point of view of the Prime Minister of the day, and it will

Bank of Canada
probably be many years to come before the other house on some of these matters of trade and finance, is at all likely to be in sympathy with a House of Commons which might be differently constituted from the present one.
In such circumstances what will the position be? If there are no directors of the bank who are appointed by the government itself and whose duty it is to protect the national interest from the point of view of the government, an incoming administration which has trade policies different from those of the present administration, unless it were so fortunate as to find in the governor of the bank a gentleman who would be quite prepared to accept the policies of the government on important national matters and seek to further them, would find itself in a position where it might not be able to carry out the very policies which the country had sent it into office to further. This is the time to mention that possibility. It is the point I brought to the Prime Minister's attention last night. I do not think he has given a satisfactory reply to it.
The obvious thing to be done in these circumstances is to provide that at least a certain number of directors shall be appointed by the government of the day, and that these directors, who will not own shares, should sit on the board to cooperate in shaping the policies of the bank and to see that at all times, with respect to great national policies, those of the bank and those of the country are brought as much as possible into common accord.

Will the right hon. gentleman permit a question in order that laymen in the house may get a clear idea of what he has in his mind? Will he suggest that the governor and deputy governor and even the directors representing the public should be changed with a change of government in this country, in other words be made political appointments? His argument suggests to me as a layman that he feels that the governor, the deputy governor and a majority of the board of directors should be changed or dismissed with each change of government.

I have said nothing about the governor and nothing about the deputy governor, so my hon. friend may set his mind at rest in that regard. It is admitted that the present Prime Minister will appoint a governor and I assume he will be a person who is sympathetic with the prime minister's fiscal and other policies. I have said nothing about the governor or the deputy governor.
As to the directors, the present proposal is that they shall all be appointed by the shareholders. No one of the directors is to be an appointee of the government. My first point is that, regardless of which party may be in office, it is advisable that the government itself should appoint some of the directors, that some of the directors should feel that their appointment is made by the government, just as other directors will feel that their appointment is made by the shareholders. The persons appointed as directors by the shareholders will doubless feel that they have a special obligation to the shareholders. Surely it might be considered just as honourable that a number of directors to be named by the government should feel that they owed a special obligation to the government of the country which has appointed them. I am suggesting that the board of directors should be divided as between those nominated by the shareholders and those nominated by the government. I suggest that course as a means of avoiding a possible conflict between the bank and the government, or between what I may describe as the money power on the one hand and the political power on the other.
I say that, if we ever come to one of those great issues into which the world is all too quickly heading, of a conflict between money power on the one hand and political power on the other, there can be but one answer to a conflict of that kind, and that is the ultimate control by the political power and not by the money power. By the provisions of this bill we are placing pretty much all control in the hands of the money power.
Does the right hon. gentleman suggest that the directors he refers to should be political directors in the sense that they should be appointed and dismissed politically
The answer is in the terms of the amendment.

I believe there are real
grounds for the fears of financial domination which have just been expressed by the right hon. leader of the opposition (Mr. Mackenzie King) but I think that the fears he expressed in regard to financial imperialism might better be discussed when we are dealing with that clause of the bill which empowers the Bank of Canada to affiliate or have relationships with the Bank of International Settlements.
As to the possibility, or likelihood-I think that is a better -way to put it-of the financial powers seeking control of the central bank, in my opinion there is every likelihood that-
Bank oj Canada

they will do so, and in trying to prevent that I have already joined with hon. gentlemen to my right in endeavouring to get this institution established on a publicly owned basis. But for reasons which the government have given in regard to a different viewpoint and a different policy they have refused to grant that, so I am not sure that the amendment now before the house would be of very much advantage. For instance, this is a private bank and there is no attempt to camouflage it as being anything else. As such the bill provides the means which are in keeping with private ownership as to how the directors and the officials shall be appointed. The amendment seeks to depart from the principle of private ownership, which is the basis of the legislation before us, and to make appointments on an entirely different basis so that if the amendment carried we would have a directors' board one-half viewing themselves from the point of view of the banking business and the other half perhaps from an entirely different viewpoint. It is just possible that in that way we would have more confusion than we would have by allowing the board of directors to be appointed as the bill assumes, on a proper private ownership basis. I can conceive that there would be times when if a clash did arise the members of the board would take advantage of that situation and blame each other instead of frankly accepting the responsibility which belonged to them as directors of the institution.
With regard to financial policy I would submit to the committee that this parliament has control of the financial policy and has stated that policy in section 25. I think that is the important feature controlling the policy of the central bank. And that is in the power of this parliament. We have not come to that section yet, however. It is not left to the governors or directors of the bank to say what principle shall direct the financial policy which the central bank is to follow. Section 25 of the act takes care of that.
I pointed out yesterday, and I think it is necessary to emphasize it again, that the central bank grants no new powers to the-financiers but rather takes some of their powers away. There can be no doubt that up to this time the chartered banks and the chartered banks' bankers have had control of both credit and currency in Canada and have' exercised any control that has been manifest-over all these years. Now this bill before the committee takes a good deal of that control out of their hands and places it in the hands of the government, and to that extent
fMr. Irvine.]
the bill is so much better than anything we-have had so far in the dominion.
Let me call the attention of the committee to the number of instances provided in this bill where powers have been taken which once were exercised by the chartered banks, powers which private institutions have been deprived of. First, the provisional board of directors must be appointed by the government. Now there was no such proviso in regard to the directors of the chartered banks when they controlled the credit of Canada. Then there are three of the permanent board of directors who are to be appointed by the government. I do not think anyone will argue that that is not an advance on what used to be the situation. Next, the first governor of the bank is to be appointed by the governor in council, and subsequent governors have to be approved by the governor in council.
I do not know whether it is proper to say what I am about to say, and if it is not I shall take it back; but the only way to find out whether it is proper or not is to say it, I think that if the government make as good appointments in connection with the governor and other officials of the bank whom they will have to appoint as they have made in the appointment of the deputy minister of finance, we shall have no cause to complain about the management of the bank.
The next provision is that the governor, the appointee of the government, has power to veto any by-laws. Next, all action of the board and the executive must be concurred in by the governor. Next, the deputy minister or a substitute for the deputy minister will be a member of the board without voting power. If it is merely desired that we should have someone there to give warning I am certain that warning will be forthcoming. The next provision is that complete regulations governing the bank have been laid down by parliament, as I have emphasized; and the most important principle in the direction of financial policy is section 25 to which I have referred. That is really the principle which will largely direct the policy the bank will follow. Then all profits except four and one-half per cent on capital invested go to the receiver general. There is another restriction which we did not find when the bankers were controlling the policy of the country; under the chartered banks they went off with all the profits they could make and therefore had only one incentive in every enterprise, namely, to . make more profits. Moreover, the commercial banks are not allowed to have financial interest in the capital stock of the present bank, and that is also a restriction of their financial control

Bank of Canada
of the country. Again, parliament's consent must be obtained before there can be an increase in the capital of the central bank, and the Minister of Finance has full control of the share personnel. Finally, no person other than the minister shall vote for more than fifty shares. These are all restrictions and curtailments of financial power which heretofore had absolutely no existence in financial legislation in Canada.
While therefore, as I have said, I wanted to see this a publicly owned bank, nevertheless I must say that my right hon. friend (Mr. Mackenzie King) and his following to the right have not had anything to say hitherto in regard to the control of the financial interests of Canada, though up to this time financiers have exercised authority, without any restriction, over the whole financial structure of the country.

Sections 10 to 13 inclusive agreed to.
On section 14-All action must be concurred in by governor or deputy.

Before we proceed with
section 14 I wash to propose an amendment, to insert a newr section, 13 (a). This is an amendment which I proposed in the committee on banking and commerce. It was considered by that committee for some time and the Minister of Finance asked that it stand and that consideration be given to it after the bill had been reported from that committee to the house. Accordingly, I will now move the amendment:
13-A. The deputy minister of finance, or in case of his absence or incapacity at any time, such other representative of the Department of Finance as the minister may name for the time being, shall, by virtue of his office or of such nomination as the case may be, have the right to protest against any act or decision of the board or of the executive committee (except a decision nominating a commissioner as hereinafter provided for) which he may consider to be contrary to law or against the interests of the state, by filing such protest in writing with the board or the executive committee as the case may be, and with the minister, and any such protest, unless the same is not concurred in by the minister within two days shall have the force of a suspensive veto so that nothing shall be done under the authority of or pursuant to such act or decision until the merits of the protest shall have been decided upon by a commission of three persons constituted as follows: one person to be named by the board and one person to be named by the minister within seven days after such protest, and one person, to be the chairman to be chosen jointly by the minister and the bank,
and in default of agreement on such last mentioned person within seven days after such protest, such chairman shall be the chief justice or acting chief justice of the Supreme Court of Canada; the decision of such commission to be made within seven days after the commission has been constituted or within such further time as the minister and the bank may agree upon and the decision of the commission shall have the full force and effect of a decision of the board of directors in respect of which no protest has been filed.
The effect of the new clause is to incorporate in this bill a provision which is found in a large number of charters constituting *central banks. I shall read the list that I have before me. It includes Austria, Czechoslovakia, Denmark, Esthonia, Germany, Greece, Hungary, Italy, Japan, Poland, Portugal, South Africa, Jugoslavia. The provision is intended for the purpose primarily of preserving state interests. One could conceive of a situation in which even the governor might vote to take a certain action and the provision is that the deputy minister, who is by this bill made a non-voting member of the board, nay if he considers such action to be against the interests of the state or contrary to law, that is contrary to the constitution of the bank, file a suspensive veto or protest with the board, and unless the suspensive veto is not concurred in by the minister within two days, that shall operate to suspend the action of the board until the difference is composed between the government and the directors of the bank.
If, of course, the provision had been carried with regard to public ownership or if the provision had been carried whereby a majority of the board were government appointed, this would not be necessary, but I am endeavouring in every way possible to have the national interests as opposed to what my right hon. leader speaks of as the money power, made dominant in connection with this organization. Therefore, if we cannot have provision whereby the national interests may take the initiative and positive action, I believe this provision helps at least to some extent to provide that the national interests may be asserted in order to prevent action which may be regarded as detrimental to the interests of the state.
As I said, this is not by any means a new provision. The Prime Minister and those who are familiar with central bank organizations will know it is contained already in a large number of acts. It seems to me that I cannot emphasize again too strongly what has already been emphasized from this side of the house, namely, that the control of the currency and credit of our dominion and the stabilization of the value of our currency
Bank of Canada

are matters which should after all be under the direct control of the state and of the government as representing the people of Canada. I therefore beg leave to move the amendment.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
I do not intend to say
anything because the matter has been fully discussed in the committee. The illustrations to which reference has been made are illustrations under conditions which are so different from ours I do not think the matter calls for any discussion, and the conclusion arrived at in the committee reflected the mind of the majority. If the deputy minister and the government in a country and democracy such as this do not take steps to protect the public interest I entirely lose my appreciation of the situation.

I do not think my right
hon. friend ought to dismiss the matter as quickly as that. The point is that the deputy minister is the one who has power to assert and protest. I do not think he is going to need it, but this is giving him power which he does not have under the bank as constituted by the legislation. At the moment he has no power except to sit in the board of directors and hold a watching brief. This gives him power to assert the interests of the state by registering a protest which has the effect of a suspensive veto in any matter which is regarded as prejudicial to the national interests.
My right hon. friend says that if the deputy minister is not sufficiently seized of the importance of the state's interests he does not see any possibility of protecting the interests of the state. The purpose of this amendment is for that very reason, to give the deputy minister power to assert the state interests as predominant over the interests of a private bank.
I should like to ask the Prime Minister this question: When the bank is set up and the deputy minister is taking his seat on the executive of the bank-
He is not a member of the executive.

He takes his seat without a vote. If something comes up with which he disagrees and he advises the government through the Minister of Finance, in what way is the government in a position to exercise influence on the governor to get the board to change their mind?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
In practice there has
never been any difficulty so far as the Bank of England is concerned, for instance, nor so

far as the Bank of France is concerned. I can only give those two illustrations. The financial policy in general of France the Bank of France has carried out from time to time except where there have been grave doubts as to government at all and matters of that sort, but the bank continued to carry out the general policy.
The Bank of England very often decided government policy.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: The hon. member for Vancouver Centre suggests that the Bank of England frequently decides the policy of the government in Great Britain. I suppose by that he means to indicate that the experience of those who are the directors of that bank and of the governor is so great and ripe that the government are glad to avail themselves of it. I cannot think of anything other than that that he can have in mind.
Morley's Life of Gladstone has several references to that.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: One can get something more recent than that if the hon. member so desires.
Ramsay MacDonald.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Yes; between 1914 and 1921 there were many cases in which it is recorded that the view at first of the officials and directors of the bank was not the same as that of the government, but in most cases the records indicate that the government after discussion accepted the view of the bank. As is pointed out in the book to which reference is made, there was no collision; there may have been differences and sometimes they were acute, but they were always adjusted.
Was there not a situation that arose when the right hon. Ramsay MacDonald was head of the government, which resulted in the resignation of his government?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: No; his government resigned on account of the Campbell case in connection with the prosecution. His government, as the right hon. gentleman will remember, resigned in consequence of the Campbell matter. That is what brought about the difficulty.

No, I mean the resignation of the Labour government just before the formation of the present national government.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: I thought the right hon. gentleman referred to the first resignation.
No.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: As to the last resignation, this is my information: the balance of trade was running so strongly against that country it became necessary in the opinion of the then chancellor of the exchequer, now Lord Snowden, that immediate action should be taken. My information, for what it may be worth-and the reminiscences so indicate-is that the bank entirely agreed as to the necessity of immediate action being taken. It will be recalled that there was a discussion that went on well into the night between the chancellor, the governor and, shall I say the city men, because the heads of some of the great banks were also consulted. In the end immediate action was thought desirable, and as is well known, Mr. MacDonald formed the national government. I do not think there was any difference of opinion; it was because of entire agreement between the bank and the then chancellor of the exchequer as to the seriousness of the situation, if my information is correct. I think probably no factor was more potent in bringing about the result than the broadcast speech of the chancellor of the exchequer, Lord Snowden, with respect to the matter.

Was there not at the outset a question of the bank indicating pretty directly the terms upon which credit could be obtained, and of what was taken to mean the only terms, and so really forcing the hands of the government in the matter?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: I dare say the sources of information of the right hon. gentleman are perhaps as full as mine, but my information is that when the situation became acute and the demand upon the bank's gold supply became very great the chancellor of the exchequer was of the opinion that something drastic should be done, and that an effort should be made to adjust balances and bring about, shall I say, a surplus in the budget. The bank pressed their position very strongly, but I think those of us who know Lord Snowden do not believe for a moment that he became acquiescent to anything other than conviction that he was doing what was right; and the speech that he made, which most people think was the determining factor in the election,-I think I can recall the matter now, although I must speak subject to correction, for I have not looked it up recently-the speech he then made over the wireless indicated that the savings of the people, the money derived from their savings certificates, was being utilized by the administration borrowing it for the purpose of supporting the so-called dole. He pointed out that it was absolutely essential that there should be a readjustment with respect to all the public services to bring about equilibrium between income and outgo. I have been told and read, but probably the right hon. gentleman has read and been told also, that that was a more decisive factor than any other in bringing about the result, in the sense that those who suffered voted for a national government, a most amazing spectacle. Perhaps the right hon. gentleman remembers the speech made about it by Mr. Churchill in which he referred to their having said, "We voted for England," and the speech made by the then Mr. Philip Snowden in which he quoted the famous lines from Swinburne.
That was his last budget speech?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
His last budget speech, yes. I do know that there is no doubt that the bank, the bank officials, do exercise a very considerable influence on the financial policy of England. But it must also be remembered that the bank is utilized as the fiscal agent of the government, and the relations between them are the relations of a government and its fiscal agent, which of course must be very intimate. This bill contemplates that this bank will act without fee as the fiscal agent of the Dominion of Canada. Therefore the relations between the bank and the Minister of Finance will necessarily be very close. This bill is predicated upon the assumption that the bank is an instrumentality of government, and that it will use its best efforts to forward the interests of whatever government there is. I think if the right hon. gentleman would pause for a moment he would realize that the argument he made a few minutes ago is destructive of his own theory; for assuming, as he says, that I appoint the governor for a term of years and he is not of the same financial school as the right hon. gentleman, and that he succeeded to office, then he would find a governor who was not in accord with his general views. The right hon. gentleman therefore suggests that the government should appoint the directors. So I appoint the directors. Where is he then? They also reflect my mind. The result is that instead of having a board of directors that may be for all I know entirely friendly to the views of the right hon. gentleman, it is not improbable
Bank oj Canada

that on a cross section of the shareholders throughout the country, with whom fifty shares is the maximum holding, there will be as many people of the viewpoint of the right hon. gentleman as there would be of mine, for instance. If you take it on the balance of probability there are perhaps those who would say there would be more. Therefore it seems to me that I have done a greater service to the right hon. gentleman by providing for this .position than if I provided that the directors should be appointed by the government and be there for a term of years. The change of administration would then find not only the governor but the board of directors set in their ways, making it much more difficult for the right hon. gentleman to deal with the situation than otherwise.
Does not the act provide that the directors retire in rotation?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Yes, but the shortest term is two years, then three, four and five years. This one further point I think may be useful in that regard. It is true that the directors retire in rotation, and they are elected from the whole body of shareholders. I have no reason to believe that they will all be of one political viewpoint, any more than the right hon. gentleman has. I think that is one of his best assurances.
Just one word more. It is erroneous to say that we are taking control away from parliament. Any parliament can be called together and do anything it pleases to this bank. The contingency that the right hon. gentleman has suggested, that the Senate might interfere, will only leave wider scope and greater opportunity for the right hon. gentleman, if the time ever comes, to exercise those reforming qualities with respect to that body that were interfered with by providence on a previous occasion.

speechtext: I wish the hon. gentleman would make that clear, because as the amendment stands it is what is here already.

To meet the wishes of
the Prime Minister I will substitute the words, "provided that each said note shall be printed in both the English and the French language."
My remarks in support of this amendment will be very brief. It is needless to argue either the legal or the constitutional issue, since, after I moved a similar amendment in the banking committee, the Minister of Finance moved the proviso that now appears in subsection 4. I am quite willing to admit that this is a recognition of the principle, and my only reason for proposing the amendment has to do with the question of method, of better policy, .perhaps even of better taste. It has been recognized by the provision inserted in the bill that since there are banks in this country issuing notes in both English and French, now that the Bank of Canada will have the exclusive privilege of issuing notes it is only fair that the notes should be issued in French as well as in English. I hardly need to refer to the fact that these notes are legal tender; they are so described in this very section. Under section 133 of the British North America Act both English and French are used in the courts, not only those of the province of Quebec but also in all the federal courts. There are federal courts in Canada; the exchequer court sits 74726-268
everywhere. So these documents, being legal tender, certainly should be issued in both languages.
As I said before, it is a question as to the best method to be followed. Everywhere in the world where a similar situation exists, in order to show the duality of language in such countries both languages, and in certain countries .three languages, are used on the notes issued by the banks. For instance, in Belgium they have both French and Flemish on the notes. In Switzerland, where there are three official languages, French, German and Italian, the notes are issued with the three languages appearing thereon, and the same thing happens wherever a similar situation exists. It is so in South Africa, in the Irish Free State and in all the other countries of the world. Canada would be the only country whose national currency would be issued in two languages but not on the same note; there would be a portion of the notes printed in English and a portion of the notes printed in French. I do not think that is a good way to do it. What would be the result? There are many in Canada who did not speak the other language until after they had reached a certain age, when they took the trouble to learn it; these would like to have both languages. So far as I am concerned I would prefer to have both languages. The French notes will be circulated largely in the province of Quebec while the English notes will be circulated principally in the other provinces. Will it be a good thing to emphasize that situation, to make Quebec more French and the rest of Canada more English? I do not think it will. With regard to other countries, do you think it would be a good thing to have notes printed exclusively in French circulated in some European countries where the people do not know the conditions here, and where it might be thought that Canada is an entirely French country?
From whatever point of view you consider it I do not think the method adopted by the government is the best method. Let us admit that it may become a cause of friction in some places; if notes are offered to some people who do not like the language in which the notes are issued there may be disagreeable incidents. There may be something said or done which would not be conducive to peace and harmony in the country. Why should we take that risk? I must apologize for showing that I have a ten dollar bill in my pocket, but I have one which I am holding in my hand. Who will suffer if the notes of the Bank of Canada are issued in the same way as the notes of the Banque Canadienne Nationale or

Bank of Canada

the Banque Provinciale du Canada, whereon appear the words "ten" and "dix," and "will pay to bearer" and "paiera au porteur"?
Give it to Hansard.

No thanks. Who would suffer if that suggestion were accepted? I cannot understand how anyone could object to the issue of notes being made with both languages on the same notes, instead of having a parcel of English notes in one place and a parcel of French notes in another. The other system is that provided through the amendment suggested by the banking and commerce committee. It is merely the matter of choice between two methods, and I plead with you, Mr. Chairman, and through you to the members of the committee, to adopt the only fair and reasonable choice, and the one which will not cause friction among Canadians.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
It is perhaps unnecessary
to say that I am not unmindful of the discussions which have taken place in the public press with respect to this matter. I am not unaware, and I fancy very few members in this chamber can be unaware, of the acute feeling which has developed through those discussions. Those in the province of Quebec who have not agreed with the views put forward by the hon. member for Quebec East (Mr. Lapointe) to the effect that the notes of the Bank of Canada should each be engraved in two languages, have been denounced publicly as traitors to their race, and have been subjected to attacks of a character which I very greatly deprecate. I therefore am not unaware of the seriousness of this situation, nor do I propose to hesitate for a single moment in directing the attention of this committee to every phase of the matter, and the reasons which now necessitate a review of the constitutional situation.
When the government was called upon to frame that section of the bill which deals with note issue it will be observed that subsection 4 of section 23 read as follows:
The form and material of the notes shall be subject to approval by the minister.
It was hoped by the use of those words to
avoid any discussions such as those which have been going on during the last few weeks in the newspapers published in this country. It was further proposed that when the section was reached the minister would indicate it was the intention of the government to follow the constitution and to provide that notes should be available engraved in both the English and French languages. Therefore it was with some degree of, shall I say regret, that one observed that on March 15 last the

hon. member for Quebec East gave notice of his intention to move an amendment in terms similar to the amendment moved to-night.
