The amendment has since been amended, and as it now appears for the consideration of this committee it states that each note shall be printed in both languages. The choice therefore is between notes printed in English and notes printed in French, or each note being

Bank of Canada
engraved in English and French. This raises a question of very serious moment, and is one which has engaged the attention of this house on previous occasions. As I said a moment ago it is a question which has involved many, many hard words being spoken and written. Section 133 of the British North America Act is as follows:
Either the English or the French language may be used by any person in the debates of the houses of the parliament of Canada and of the houses of the legislature of Quebec; and both those languages shall be used in the respective records and journals of those houses; and either of those languages may be used by any person or in any pleading or process in or issuing from any court of Canada established under this act, and in or from all or any of the courts of Quebec.
The acts of the parliament of Canada and of the legislature of Quebec shall be printed and published in both those languages.
The interpretation of that section, so far as I know, has not been a matter for judicial consideration, but by common consent those who are members of this parliament have always been enabled on request to secure the proceedings of this parliament, whether in the form of debates, bluebooks or otherwise, in the French language, and equally in the English language. There was therefore an equality so far as these things were concerned. I shall refer to one debate in particular that engaged the attention of the house, that of the twenty-fifth of February, 1907, when a motion was moved by the gentleman who is now the Deputy Speaker, and there participated in that debate the hon. member for Labelle. It is a matter of satisfaction to know that twenty-seven years after that resolution was moved in this house on another matter the question now raised is being considered and the gentlemen to whom I refer, who were present twenty-seven years ago, are present this evening. The motion read as follows;
That it is in the interest and for the -wellbeing of the dominion, and in accord with the spirit of the confederation agreement of 1867, that the French language, which in virtue of the constitution is official, be placed on a footing of equality with the English language in all public matters-for instance, in the coinage of moneys and in the administration of postal affairs.
The words, it will be observed, are, "be placed on a footing of equality with the English language." To that on the twenty-fifth of February Sir Wilfrid Laurier moved in amendment:
That all the words after "that" be struck out and the following be substituted in place thereof:
74726-268J
"The French language is, in fact, as well as by the constitution, on a footing of equality with the English language.
In the course of the debate Sir Wilfrid Laurier used these words;
Of course, there are some great occasions in which it-
The French language.
-must be spoken, there are occasions of a public character when it ought to be spoken. But to affirm, as he does, that the French language should be used upon every occasion, and that every public document should be printed on one side in French and the other side in English is, I think, going a little too far. For instance, I understand that my hon. friend wants bank notes to be printed either in French or in English.
Note the words, "either in French or in English":
For my part I never yet saw an occasion where a bank note printed in English was not properly understood by the French people; and I am quite sure that a bank note printed in French would be understood by the English people to be exactly what it means. But I see no reason why a bank note should not be printed in French. Since we have been in office we have not had occasion to issue a new form of bank notes, we have taken the old form as we found it, we have continued the form of the old bank notes. I do not see any reason why, if we were to issue a new form, we should issue it in one language rather than another. But I would say to my hon. friend that it is far better that we should be conservative in these matters and not to change our forms every now and then.
For nine years the hon. gentleman who has just spoken occupied high office, and in 1930 just before leaving office a contract was entered into between the government and the bank note company that engraves Canadian bank notes, and provision was made for the engraving of all the notes that this country requires for a period of five years, the notes of the Dominion of Canada, notes for $50, $100, $500, $1,000, for all the notes that were legal tender in Canada and are the notes of the Dominion of Canada, including also the one dollar bills, the banks not having any power to issue such; also the two dollar bills and the four dollar bills, and of course the five dollar bills as well, although the banks have power to issue bills from five dollars upwards. Was any such provision as is now mentioned in this amendment contained in that contract?
There was no Bank of Canada then.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
There was the Dominion of Canada whose notes were the same as the Bank of Canada's notes. Was any such effort made to do that then? No. Therefore, sir,
Bank oj Canada

is it unfair to say that it is quite apparent that this has nothing to do with a question of business but it is a political issue pure and simple?
I deny that. I throw that back in your teeth.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
I make it perfectly clear, Mr. Chairman, that if after nine years in office the hon. gentleman raised no such question in this house, did not assert for a single moment the desirability of following the course which is now being adopted by this government, did not even approach the matter, why is it other than a political question when now, after the government has indicated it proposes to follow the constitution and engrave the notes in English and in French, we should be met by a motion that each note must be engraved in both languages?
It is a very serious matter. It is one of the most serious that this country has had to consider for a long time in view of the discussions that have been taking place in the public press of Quebec. Shall those who sit on one side of the house and follow the constitution be branded as traitors in the Liberal press? That is what has been going on in this country, and confronted with that situation this government, desiring to follow the course which I mapped out for myself when I was elected leader of this party-when I went to the old province of Quebec in the first speech that I made there I said "I propose to follow the constitution. With respect to your rights and your privileges, everything that the constitution affords to you as a minority or as a majority I propose to observe."
Nothing is more fatal than a departure from a constitutional right. Nothing is more fatal than an effort to impose upon a majority the will of a minority if the rights are established by law. Since when has it become the law of Canada that the will of a minority shall prevail over that of the majority? Since when did it become conducive to the rights of minorities that they should insist that the constitution should be disregarded and the rights of majorities taken from them? That is the question. It was that that was in the mind of Sir Wilfrid Laurier when he said, "I see no reason why one language should be preferred over the other." It was that that was in the mind of that great French Canadian when he said that equality was guaranteed by the constitution. As I intimated in my first address in the province of Quebec, by that I stand; by that this government stands or falls. Equality under the law. Equal
IMr. Bennett.]
rights. The notes in French, the notes in English; engraved in French, engraved in English, even as Sir Wilfrid Laurier said.
On July 1 next this country will celebrate the sixty-seventh anniversary of our confederation. Successive governments have come and gone; successive prime ministers have come and gone; successive parliaments have been elected and have disappeared; but for the first time in a statute of this country dealing with the question of the issue of dominion notes this government has placed a minority on the basis of equality under the law. And what is more, the hon. gentleman who has just taken his seat intimated in the committee that in the amendment moved by the Minister of Finance there was a fulfilment of the constitution, and he nods his head now in acquiescence.

He said
so to-night.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
He not only asks this '
committee to afford equality under the law by concurring in the amendment proposed by the government, which was their original intention under the section as it reads, so that there would be no controversy or discussion, but having projected the question into the debate he has admitted that the proposals of the government met the constitutional obligation. Who says nay to that? No one. Then, sir, my statement to this house is that no man is doing justice to bis own people and to the future who suggests that there should [DOT] -be inequality under the law. Equality is provided for by statute; equality is provided for by the government-equality under the law, the engraving of a French note, of an English note: equality. But the hon. member for Quebec East says: No, no; not that, not equality. I now demand that the constitution shall be amended, disregarded, flouted, and that this committee shall, instead of following it, maintaining the rights of minorities in all their strength and vigor under the law, substitute therefor disobedience to the constitution, disregard for it in any event, and that equality, as established by law, shall be departed from.
That is what we are asked to do; that is what my fellow Canadians from Quebec are asked to do. But the history of the world in dealing with the rights of minorities is clear-that when you invite any parliament to disregard the rights of majorities by pressing for rights which are not granted by the constitutions, you thereby invite a departure from the rights granted by the constitution. That is what you do. And to-night we are asked to vote for a resolution which is an

Bank of Canada
invitation to take action subversive of the rights of minorities as granted by the constitution. I will not do it. My promise was clear and it will be observed. This government stands or falls by the maintenance under the law of equality to those to whom the constitution has granted equality under the terms of section 133. By that we stand; by that we fall. And, as the years go by, when we think of the agitation now being carried on for amendments to the British North America Act, and the manner in which we have steadily stood by the rights of minorities as guaranteed by the constitution, when we recollect the statements made as to the contractual obligations of the constitution, how are the members of this committee to go out and say to the people of this country that we asked parliament to disregard these contractual rights, if they be such? That is the question; that is the question stripped of everything.
Our statutes for years have been published in separate volumes; our order paper every day appears in the English and French languages; our Hansard appears in the English and French languages; all documents which any member has a right to see, to read, to possess, he may receive in either language. And having regard to that provision, I suggest that hon. members should think carefully before they disregard the provision of the law, so clear, which for sixty-seven years has been observed-observed, mark you. In 1896 I supported the remedial measure and I have never offered apologies for having done so, because under the constitution it was provided that this parliament should take action in the event of certain contingencies. When the privy council said that those contingencies had arisen, when they so declared and this action was taken, I supported it. And in the old province of Quebec to-day the proceedings of the legislature are printed in separate volumes. I go into the library and receive statutes in English and in French. I receive reports from day to day of various departments, and some of them are so beautiful-illustrations and typography -that one values them apart altogether from the information they contain. Moreover, in that legislature bills are printed in English and in French.
I do not propose to labour the question. I have endeavoured to intimate to the committee the principles that have governed us in our approach to this matter. It has not been lightly done; it has not been done in caprice nor for political reward nor hope of reward. It has been done because we thought
and still believe that under the section I have read, the minister approving of the form and material, these notes should be issued. When this amendment seeks to impose, as it does, not equality under the law but a certain form by which, however small the bill, there shall be engraved upon it two languages and not that the bill may be available in either, the committee, I do submit, has a very serious responsibility.
I am not going to dwell further upon the matter. My duty is to discharge my obligations to my fellow citizens under the constitution, and that I will do. And when I see my fellow citizens from Quebec, who have been subjected to these attacks in the daily press, so vicious in character, so uncalled for, denounced as traitors to their race because they dare to assert their constitutional rights as members, rather than endeavour to obtain for themselves other than the equality which the law provides, I ask-[DOT] is it fair, is it right, is it just? When we have observed the constitution-observed it, mark you, for the hon. member for Quebec East admits that-then why project this question into the discussion if not for political reasons? Why do it? That having been done, I cannot but think that the responsibility for it is one which those who have created and must accept it will live long enough some day to regret.

After what we have listened to from the Prime Minister, I think it might be well to remind the committee of the section which is under consideration, and of the exact nature of the amendment which has been moved. The subsection under discussion reads:
The form and material of the notes shall be subject to approval by the minister: Provided that notes in either the English or the French language shall be available as required.
The words, "that notes in either the English or the French language shall be available as required," are words which were put there by the government of the day. The Prime. Minister himself has stated to us this evening that his government is responsible for that provision. The provision is that there shall be notes in English and in French. In so doing the Prime Minister says that he has followed the constitution.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: That is admitted.

He has said repeatedly that the hon. member for Quebec East (Mr. Lapointe) in the amendment he has moved has admitted that the right hon. gentleman as Prime Minister has in what he is doing followed the constitution and observed
Bank of Canada

all constitutional obligations. My right hon. friend has, however, gone on to say that the hon. member for Quebec East now demands that the constitution should be amended. Can my right hon. friend substantiate that statement?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Certainly.
The hon. member for Quebec East makes and has made no demand for any amendment of the constitution.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Certainly.

Not at all.
Nothing is further from the mind of the hon. member for Quebec East; he has made no request for any amendment of the constitution. The amendment that is before the committee at the present moment is one which relates to the method by which the requirements of the constitution may be carried out so as best to serve the convenience of the public and best to make for harmony and good-will between the different elements of the country. The Prime Minister's method of complying with the constitution is to issue two sets of notes, some in French and some in English; that is what the provision of this bill now under consideration requires. The method which the hon. member for Quebec East proposes is that the notes should bear on the face of them as to their denomination the French as well as the English language. The question is simply one of the method which will best serve the convenience of the people of the country and make for harmony; there is no question of the constitution in the matter. It must be a relief to the Prime Minister to find that I am not arguing for adherence to the constitution at present. He is the one who is asserting that particular aspect. But it is quite clear that what is involved here is simply a difference of method in issuing notes, having regard to what will best serve the public convenience and national unity.
May I ask hon. members: What, apart from all other considerations, would, as a matter of fact to most of us who are English speaking, be the most convenient method to have followed as respects moneys that are to issue from this central bank assuming, as is to be the case, that it is going to issue all the currency? Will it be more convenient for us to receive our payments in bills, some wholly in French and others wholly in English, or will it be more convenient, whenever a bill is received, to find that its denomination is in both languages? That is the whole question. These bills will circulate from one

end of Canada to the other; when payments are made in different localities, bills in French must be accepted equally with bills in English, because each are legal tender. Is it not going to make for greater convenience all round that, when moneys are sent from one part of Canada to another, there should be no possibility of any question arising -when a bill is received, because of its being in one language rather than in another, because having the two languages on its face it will be readily understood by all, than rather, as will otherwise frequently happen, sometimes understood by some and often not understood by large numbers of persons. Think too of the inconvenience to local banks all over Canada which will have two sets of notes, one set in French and one in English. That is the whole question.
The Prime Minister said-and I resent very strongly the statement he made-that the hon. member for Quebec East was trying to raise a political issue.
That is an infamous lie.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
The hon. gentleman's
language will have to be altered. He is not holding a meeting somewhere. He said that something is an infamous lie. He must withdraw that language.
Mr. Chairman-

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
I am raising a point of
order and I must press it.
There has been a great deal of talk-

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: He is trying to get away from it but this is something he cannot get away from. He must withdraw those words.

I said that anyone who
said I am doing this from a political point of view utters an infamous lie. I said that. I did not mention anybody in particular, but I will withdraw the statement if it is against the rules of the house.

I was saying,
when I was interrupted by the Prime Minister, that he stated that the hon. member for Quebec East was seeking to raise a political issue. May I say that the one who is seeking to raise a political issue is the Prime Minister himself and that his whole speech this evening was an effort to raise a political issue.
In order that the committee may get back again to the real point, which is the one involved in the amendment, the question of public convenience, of what is the best method and what is likely to serve the interests of

Bank of Canada
good will and harmony as between all parts and all races of this country, may I refer to what has taken place with respect to the postage of Canada. Unlike my hon. friend the member for Quebec East, I do not happen to have a ten dollar bill in my pocket; but I have a two cent stamp.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Is it not a five?
A five cent piece.

I am sorry I have not a five cent piece, but 1 have a two cent stamp and I notice that the wording upon it appears in both English and French. I happen to have a three cent stamp as well, so that we are getting to the five cents by degrees. This is not a postage, but a national revenue stamp a three cent excise stamp, and I find that it also is in both English and French. Both of these, the excise stamp and the postage stamp, are issued by the present administration. As I understand it, all the postage stamps and also all the excise stamps of Canada also the postal notes and money orders are at present being issued by the government in both languages. This is being done for what reason? Because of a belief in equality. I wish to ask hon. members, if they are interested in equality, and what is the most obvious manner of asserting equality, whether the evidence of equality is not greater in a document or token that on its face is printed in the two languages rather than in what is proposed by this measure, namely, two sets of documents or tokens, one in one language and the other in the other postage or revenue stamps or money orders or postal notes or bank notes issued as is proposed in the amendment rather than as is proposed in the provision of this bill as drafted by the government. I do not think it is necessary to say more than that. I have no desire to indulge in heroics. If one wished to follow the Prime Minister it would not be difficult in a discussion on this subject to rouse very quickly many racial passions. The hon. member for Quebec East in his remarks made it very clear that what he was seeking to do was not to raise a political issue but to avoid political issues being raised.
Oh, oh.

Hon. members should take the trouble to read in Hansard tomorrow what the hon. member for Quebec East said, as they could not possibly have heard him or they would not be jeering at the moment. He said that in the event, in some parts of Canada, of notes in French being
handed to someone unable to speak the French language, difficulties and unpleasantnesses might arise between the party tendering the notes and the one asked to receive them. In directing attention to that, was my hon. colleague trying to create a political issue or was he trying to prevent political issues from arising? That was and is his sole purpose. These notes are going to be circulated in largest numbers, may I point out, in the largest financial and urban centre we have in this country, the city of Montreal. Out of that city to other parts of Canada will flow a larger number of the notes of the Bank of Canada than from any other centre in Canada. Is it not probable that a very large proportion of those notes from the city of Montreal will be notes printed in French? I should like to know whether good will and harmony between the two races and all parts of the country, and that good understanding which is at the basis of everything previous in our national life, will not be better preserved by having these notes go out bearing on their face the denomination in both languages, rather than large quantities going out in French and other large quantities in English. That sums up pretty much the whole question that is before us.
In conclusion I submit it is extraordinary that the Prime Minister of this country should seek to make a political issue out of a matter of this kind and that in so doing he should direct a personal attack upon the hon. member for Quebec East. I wish to say that there i? no man in Canada. I do not care to which side of the house we look, who has done more in the course of his life to further good will as between all races and classes in this country than my hon. colleague the former Minister of Justice. And I say further that there is not an hon. member of the parliament of Canada, either of the present or any previous parliament, who has done as much in his life to further international good will as has my hon. friend the former Minister of Justice. It ill becomes the Prime Minister to try to attribute to one so experienced and so honoured in our public life a motive as low and base as that which the Prime Minister has nut forward, a motive which the member for Quebec East is incapable of thinking of, let alone acting upon, in any personal or public matter.

It seems to me that in this heated debate we are losing sight of what I might call the broad, practical aspect of this question. As a political issue-well let us be
Bank of Canada

frank about it, all political leaders and all politicians are endeavouring to make the best they can out of every question. In my experience, it has always been done, and provided it is done honestly and honourably nobody can find fault with that, and no party should throw stones at the other. The hon. member for Quebec East (Mr. Lapointe), in all sincerity-in that regard I entirely endorse what the leader of the opposition (Mr. Mackenzie King) has said-in his sincere desire to present the question in the least passionate manner has somewhat minimized the issue. But I am afraid that on the other side the Prime Minister (Mr. Bennett) disquieted as he rightly is, from appearance at least, by the tone of some of the papers in the province of Quebec, has rather exaggerated what 1 would call the electoral or racial aspect of this question. I have known the province of Quebec for a long while. I do not believe that the exalted tone of some of the papers in the province of Quebec represents the feelings of the sensible mass of the people.
Hear, hear.

The average French
Canadian farmer or artisan or business man is prepared to take all the dollars he can earn and make the best use of them, especially at the present time, whether they are printed in French or English or Chinese or any other language. I also believe that some of those staunch supporters of British rights-"this is an English country, nothing but English"-* would not spit on a bill printed in French if it helped them in buy'ing a bottle of Scotch whisky. So I do not take very seriously that aspect of the question.
But there are serious aspects. I shall not discuss the constitutional issue. If I ventured to express an opinion on what I might call the legal aspect, I am afraid the Prime Minister is absolutely right. I think the amendment as framed by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Rhodes) conforms strictly to the letter of article 133 of the British North America Act.
We all agree to that.

Of course the ex-Minister of Justice, with his knowledge of law, admits it. That does away with three-quarters of those extravagant and heated expressions of opinion which appeared in the irresponsible papers of the province of Quebec; and in the province of Quebec, as elsewhere, most of the papers are irresponsible. It was stated that this amendment of the Minister 
of Finance is a step backward. Of course I have a very simple mind and a limited experience both in reading law and in parliamentary government, but I cannot get it into my head that this legislation, declaring for the first time that bills and money shall be printed in French, is a backward step in the acknowledgment of the French language. But I leave that aside also. I simply ask the members of this committee, on both sides of the house, to think of a broader aspect which relates to the principle of the issuing of currency. For centuries past as well as in present times, in every country, the issue of currency, the means of exchange between individuals, is an exercise of the right of sovereignty. Therefore the bills or coins which represent that means of exchange should first bear the stamp of the sovereign. In this respect it will be a great advantage to do away with those bills that are at present going right and left having on them pictures of many gentlemen, some of them good, honest people, some of them
Less honest.

-high-class crooks who should foe in peniteniaries, but whose pictures occupy the place of that of the sovereign on these bills of exchange which we call money. Therefore I hope the next bills will bear the stamp of the king-not the king of England, not the emperor of the British Empire, but the king of Canada, as we acknowledge him.
Who is that?

It is King George for
the time being. Where is the hon. member from? So long-I say it for my hon. friend's satisfaction-as we think proper to consider King George as our king. Now the other more modern significance of coins and money bills is to express nationality. In our day sovereignty and nationality are supposed to work together, and money bills, as postage stamps, which circulate the world over, which the nationals of any country carry with them when they travel abroad, are supposed to signify that the country from which those postage stamps or bills come is governed by this or that sovereign, or this or that institution, if it is a republic, and that it is peopled by individuals speaking a certain language. Now, whether we like it or not, this country was for a century and a half a French speaking country. After the conquest and cession it continued to be French speaking under a foreign government. The rulers of Great Britain, at a period when racial and religious prejudices were much

Bank of Canada
stronger than they are to-day, were nevertheless convinced that it was impossible for a conquering power to rule a foreign nation composed of civilized beings according to the tenets and with the use of the language of the conquering nation. So that even under that old, stubborn king, George III, they acknowledged the French language as the language of civil life and even of legal life in Canada. And, with a slight interruption in 1840, when the French language was suppressed by an act of the British parliament, the French language has remained one of the official languages of Canada.
In Belgium, as the hon. member for Quebec East pointed out, both the Flemish and the French languages are official. The language of the majority is Flemish, but the right of the Walloon minority to speak its language has been observed. There, curiously enough, it is the majority that has had to fight for the expression of its rights in various matters of administration which I need not relate to-night. In Switzerland there is a large majority of German speaking people; about one-third of the population is French speaking and there is an extremely small minority of Italian speaking people. Do not imagine that those people always agreed on language or racial matters. I happened to be in Switzerland just about a week before the war broke out. In French Switzerland the sympathy for France was just as strongly expressed as the sympathy for Germany was expressed in German Switzerland. There have been quarrels, quibblings and difficulties in the use of languages in Switzerland, as we have had them here. Nevertheless, belonging to an old civilization and having old traditions, they realized that it must not be a matter of oppression by one as against the other, and they have settled once for all that those documents expressing the broad nationality of the people should bear testimony to the understanding which has existed between them for centuries. Therefore their money bears all three languages. That is not the case with their postage stamps, because it would be too complicated to have three languages on postage stamps. So they agreed on one word, the Latin word Helvetia, which expresses the name of the country for the three nationalities. On all other documents the three languages are used.
Now let us come back to our present situation in Canada. When I have discussed this issue-and I have discussed it often in the last thirty years, not only in parliament but still more frequently before English speaking audiences in Ontario, Manitoba, Saskatchewan and even British Columbia-I have never
presented the question as a constitutional matter or as a question of right on the part of French Canadians. That is where I think most of our fellow citizens in the province of Quebec, especially in those heated expressions of opinion appearing in the press or occurring during speeches, are wrong. Why put it on, the basis of law? Why put it on the basis of a right exacted by the minority, if possible, from the majority, instead of basing it on common sense, in the general interests of Canada? In all those matters which express in material fashion the characteristics of the Canadian nation there has been the constant thought in my mind that if we want to preserve this confederation of ours for the generations to come, whether they speak French or English, German or Polish or any other language; or whether we consider it primarily from a British point of view as one of the "essential elements of the British Empire, let us not forget that the everlasting obstacle, to that preservation is the constant and tremendous penetration of American thought, American civilization, American language and American influences of all sorts. I have always considered that everything which tends to differentiate the Canadian nationality from the American nationality, and show to the outside world, to the passer-by, to the traveller, whether he is of English, German or French origin, that we want to express the difference of our civilization and its component elements from that of the United States, should be encouraged.
What is the main difference between Canada and the United States? Is it climate? Is it production? Is it social habits? Is it literature? That may be the case to a large extent in the province of Quebec, though I am sorry to say that it becomes less so from day to day. As regards English speaking Canada, however, let my good friends on all sides of the house make what we call in Catholic theology their examination in conscience. Do they realize to what extent from year to year their children are becoming more and more American? Do they realize that the so-called American literature of the cheapest kind is being circulated in Canada to a degree to which the circulation of English literature cannot be compared? I admit that in connection with a small measure of this nature we cannot counteract that influence, but I repeat that everything should be encouraged which will remind the children of Ontario, of Quebec, of New Brunswick or of Saskatchewan that Canada is something different from the United States, that in Canada there are elements of ethnical, culture
Bank of Canada

and social civilization which differentiates the Canadian nation as a whole from the great American nation to the south. Do you not think that is the best permanent service we can render not only to ourselves and not only to Canada but, I repeat, to the British Empire?
It is not by the strength of arms, by the influence of money or by diplomacy that Great Britain has kept Canada within her great empire. We have remained a part of the British Empire because, after many years of misunderstandings, England succeeded in gaining the confidence of that portion of the Canadian nation which is of French origin, which speaks French and which desires, not in a spirit of arrogance but on the contrary in a spirit of confraternity, to stamp its character on the nation with its language, not to the detriment of the English language or of English culture but rather in unison with English culture. We do not desire to do what the Norman conquerors did in England. They imposed the French language on the great English nation for five centuries, but that did not prevent English civilization from emerging out of that conquest and developing that magnificent policy with which we are all proud to be associated. In this country of ours, principles of liberty and cooperation should prevail over any idea of the imposition of the will of a majority on the minority or the arrogant demand of a minority from an unwilling majority. Whether we belong to the majority or the minority, let us all consider these things from a broad Canadian point of view, from a broad British point of view and from a broad international point of view.
I repeat that in a small matter of this kind we cannot do a great deal, but by this means every Canadian, wherever he may travel, will show that under the sovereignty of King George, which we freely acknowledge -not because he is the king of England but because he is our king and because we wish to keep him our king-we have freedom to express ourselves in French or in English, and that our civilization is the result of the unison, the amity and the cooperation of those two great races. Do you not think it is better to have that expressed every time and everywhere than to leave it to the narrow interpretation of the French speaking Canadian or the narrow interpretation of the English speaking Canadian to say, on one side, "we are French" and on the other "we are English"? Let us say, "we are all Canadians," and we make use of those two great instruments of civilization, those two great expressions of human thought, the

French language and the English language, to prove to the world that two races can live in amity, can understand each other, can make concessions to each other without always quibbling about legal texts or endeavouring to show that a majority is oppressing a minority or that a minority is endeavouring to wrest, through political squabbles and intrigues, privileges for which it should not ask. It is in that spirit, Mr. Chairman, that twenty-seven years ago, as the Prime Minister has reminded us, I upheld with quite the same degree of fervour the request of the hon. member for Mont-magny (Mr. LaVergne). It is in the same spirit that ill through my somewhat agitated life I have always endeavoured to bring the French Canadian to understand the English and the English to understand the French Canadian, because so long as we do not understand each other we will not accomplish anything good, but if we do understand each other we can accomplish wonders.
